label: Pappos's Theorem
notes: Welcome to Chapter 1, printed pages 3 through 32. One incidence theorem opens the entire book. Two lines, six points, three forced collinear meets. We will revisit it nine ways, watching each proof preview a different layer of projective machinery the rest of the course develops in full.

label: The Configuration
notes: Fix two lines, place three points on each. Cross the joins: A to B-prime and A-prime to B, and the two other crossed pairs. Those three intersection points are the claim. Stress that nothing forces collinearity by eye; it is a genuine theorem we must prove, not a drawing accident.

label: Incidence as Linear Algebra
notes: Here is the computational dictionary the notebook builds on. Points are homogeneous vectors up to scale, a line through two points is their cross product, two lines meet at a cross product, and three points are collinear exactly when their bracket determinant vanishes. This single dictionary powers most of the nine proofs.

label: Projective Completion
notes: Euclidean geometry treats parallels as an exception with no meeting point. Projective completion removes that exception: parallel lines meet at infinity, a homogeneous point with third coordinate zero. As slope tends to zero the finite intersection escapes like one over slope, but the homogeneous limit stays well defined on the line at infinity.

label: Proof I: Menelaus and Ratios
notes: The first classical proof is Euclidean. Apply the theorem of Menelaus to a triangle cut by transversals, multiply the signed segment ratios around the figure, and watch the auxiliary factors cancel. What survives is the ratio condition that forces the three points onto one line. Note the dependence on sign cases and an auxiliary triangle.

label: Proof II: Oriented Areas
notes: The area proof replaces fragile ratios with signed polynomials. A surrounding quadrangle area equals a signed sum of triangle and quadrangle tiles. When the hypotheses force four of those signed areas to vanish, the remaining area must vanish too, which is precisely the collinearity. Signed areas handle every sign case in one stroke.

label: Proof III: The Bracket Proof
notes: Now the projective heart. Build each intersection point as a meet, itself a cross product of two joins. Collinearity of the three results is one determinant, the bracket of their homogeneous vectors. The notebook verifies symbolically that this bracket vanishes identically, not merely in a single drawing, with SymPy confirming the exact zero.

label: Grassmann-Plucker Relations
notes: Why does the bracket vanish? Because brackets are not independent: they satisfy the Grassmann-Plucker relations, quadratic identities among three-by-three determinants. Pappos is a single instance where these relations force one bracket to zero given that the others encode the points lying on the two starting lines. This is the algebra the whole book exploits.

label: Variation I: Pascal's Theorem
notes: A pair of lines is a degenerate conic. Pascal's theorem says six points on any conic give a collinear hexagon of crossed meets, the Pascal line. Let the conic degenerate into two lines and Pascal becomes Pappos exactly. The Pascal line survives the degeneration, so Pappos is Pascal wearing a two-line costume.

label: Variation II: Cayley-Bacharach
notes: The second conic variation is stronger. Two cubics meet in nine points; if six lie on a conic, the remaining three lie on a line. The proof factors a pencil cubic as conic times residual line. Once the conic divides out, a linear factor remains, so its residual zeros are forced collinear. Pappos is a shadow of this principle.

label: Variation III: Miquel and Cross-Ratio
notes: The circle variation changes the completion. Treat lines as circles and characterize ordinary circles by the two complex circular points at infinity. Four points are cocircular exactly when a cross-ratio is real. In Miquel's configuration each assumed circle contributes a real cross-ratio, so the final four points are cocircular by the same cancellation logic.

label: Synthesis
notes: One theorem, many faces: incidence, Euclidean parallels, signed areas, a vanishing bracket, Pascal's degeneration, Cayley-Bacharach, and Miquel through cross-ratios. The recurring discipline is to never trust the drawing alone. Represent the objects, compute the incidence relation, and check the invariant the proof promises must survive every deformation.
